STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
GAVIN NEWSOM, Governor 
 
DEPARTMENT OF VETERANS AFFAIRS 
 
1227 O Street 
Sacramento, California 95814

September 3, 2025 
 
 
 
VIA ELECTRONIC TRANSMISSION  
 
The Honorable Douglas A. Collins  
Secretary, U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Ave. NW  
Washington, DC 20420  
 
The Honorable Dr. Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Under Secretary for Health, Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Ave. NW,  
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Re: Comments on Reproductive Health Services (RIN 2900-AS31)  
 
Dear Secretary Collins and Acting Under Secretary Lieberman:  
The California Department of Veterans Affairs (CalVet) submits these comments in 
opposition to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposed rule entitled 
“Reproductive Health Services,” published in the Federal Register on August 4, 2025 
(RIN 2900-AS31). CalVet’s mission is to ensure California’s veterans and their families 
receive the state and federal benefits they have earned through military service, 
including a full range of health services through the VA health care system. These 
health services must, at the bare minimum, include currently permitted abortion-
related care for qualified patients facing rape, incest, and health threats.1 This 
proposed rule eliminates the current rule’s limited exemptions to the prohibition on the 
coverage of abortion-related care, drawing the VA out of alignment with other 
federal agencies that provide or cover reproductive care.2 It is unconscionable that 
the VA would consider barring access to a critical healthcare service for the 
individuals who served their country and the family members who supported them. 
The proposed rule does not even contain a clearly-stated exemption to the prohibition 
for circumstances threatening a veteran’s life.3 The unstated “life of the mother”

17/subject-group-ECFRf01c7718f2a7e24/section-17.38 
2 "Federal Support for Reproductive Health Services: Frequently Asked Questions." Congress.gov, Library of Congress, 
1 September 2025, https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46785.

HONORING CALIFORNIA’S VETERANS 
exemption notwithstanding, assuming the VA intends to honor the silent carveout, 
CalVet has serious concerns about practical implementation in the VA medical 
facilities and affiliated community care providers throughout the nation. The rule itself 
is also dangerously vague as it relates to life-saving abortions for veterans. For the 
following reasons, CalVet strongly urges to rescind proposed rule RIN 2900-AS31: 
1. It is Unclear Whether the Amendment to § 17.38 Permits Abortions and Abortion 
Counseling in Any Circumstance.   
While the supplementary information provided by the VA assures that the 
department has never historically interpreted its regulation, even in forms identical 
to the proposed rule, to prohibit providing care to pregnant patients in life-threating 
circumstances, it declines to explicitly carve out the exemption in the section 
pertaining to the veteran’s medical benefits package.4 Instead, while the proposed 
amendments to the § 17.272 CHAMPVA health benefits program provision explicitly 
permit coverage when a physician certifies that the life of the patient would be 
endangered if the fetus were carried to term, the § 17.38 veterans medical benefits 
package lacks a similar carveout. Even the supplementary information statement 
fails to make any assurance that life-threatening conditions would be covered 
under its rule, only that these circumstances would not be excluded from 
coverage. It is absurd to purport to avoid “doubt” about the application of its rule 
by citing quoted text not found in the proposed rule itself.5 Should the VA intend to 
permit abortion “when a physician certifies that the life of the mother would be 
endangered if the fetus were carried to term,” it should explicitly include this 
exemption. Should the VA elect not to rescind RIN 2900-AS31, CalVet requests VA 
amend the proposed rule to reflect its stated intent.  
2. If the VA Employs the “Life of the Mother” Exemption in Both Circumstances, It 
Will Be Dangerously Difficult for Physicians to Implement.  
The "life of the mother" exception does not cover situations where a pregnant 
person’s health is in jeopardy, and such ambiguity has created obstacles for 
doctors providing care. In jurisdictions where abortion restrictions currently contain 
similar emergency exemptions, health care professionals are faced with making a 
fine line determination between what constitutes a circumstance with potentially 
dire health implications and one where the patient’s life is imminently threatened. 
Furthermore, the proposed rule’s condition that the “physician certifies that the life 
of the mother would be endangered” is more limiting than many other similar life 
exemptions that give greater deference to a physician’s judgement.6 The fact that 
 
4 Id.  
5 Id.  
6 38 CFR Part 17 RIN 2900-AS31 (2025) (emphasis added).  
 
Under Texas Health & Safety Code § 170A.002(b)(2), the statute defines a life-threatening physical condition and 
explicitly ties the exception to physicians’ judgment. Similarly, in Arizona, A.R.S. § 36 2321(7) defines “medical 
emergency” as: “…based on the physician’s good faith clinical judgment, either a condition … so complicates the 
medical condition of a pregnant woman as to necessitate the immediate abortion … to avert her death, or for 
which a delay … will create serious risk of substantial and irreversible impairment of a major bodily function.” 

 
HONORING CALIFORNIA’S VETERANS 
the provision has no reference to the physician’s reasonable medical judgement 
will certainly have a chilling effect on a practitioner’s willingness to make such a 
certification. The VA proposed rule should be amended to grant that deference 
and to give greater clarity regarding what constitutes life endangerment. As 
written, the lack of specificity certainly risks pregnant or miscarrying patients being 
denied or delayed treatment or coverage until they can demonstrate that their life 
is in peril. For both the CHAMPVA and the Veteran’s health benefits programs, the 
VA should provide additional specificity defining in what circumstances the VA will 
provide or approve coverage for care.  
3. After a Condition is Certified, Delays, Travel, and Administrative Hurdles Present 
Additional Barriers to Care.  
CalVet is also gravely concerned that, even when a physician certifies that the life 
of the patient is endangered, veterans and their families will not be able to access 
life-saving medical care in time to save the patient’s life. Under the current rule, 
veterans are able to obtain abortion counseling and abortion care at a VA facility 
or through the use of VA-approved community care. VA also covers the travel 
expenses to receive abortion care. Under the proposed rule change, it is unclear 
where and how VA will provide life-saving care in the limited and specific 
circumstances that will still be available to patients. CalVet is concerned that 
absent specific details, both patients and VA physicians and employees will 
struggle to understand what care is available in life-threatening circumstances, 
who (VA or a community provider) will administer care and what costs VA will 
cover. These ambiguities add an additional layer of uncertainty and procedural 
red-tape that at-risk pregnant people cannot afford.  
 
Additionally, given the high prevalence of complex service connected disabilities 
attributable to factors such as military sexual trauma and toxic exposures, women 
veterans are more likely to face high risk pregnancies and a greater incidence of 
negative birth outcomes then their non veteran peers.  It is imperative that VA 
continues to provide the timely, effective reproductive healthcare, including 
abortion care, that they have earned through their military service, or at the very 
least, in circumstances where their lives are in danger.  
 
While the VA asserts that this restriction on abortion care is merely a reversion to its 
previous rule and a long-held interpretation of that regulation, it is doing so in a post-
Dobbs decision world, which made the 2022 rule change necessary in the first place.7 
To deny such services in the post-Dobbs landscape is to deny healthcare benefits to a 
significant population of VA and CHAMPVA patients nationwide. More than 400,000 
veterans of reproductive age live in states that have heavily restricted or banned 
 
7  Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Org., 597 U.S. 215 (2022) holding that no right to abortion is implicitly protected 
by any constitutional provision, resulting in a flurry of state legislative abortion restriction.   

 
HONORING CALIFORNIA’S VETERANS 
abortion care.8  Even referrals for community care will be extremely difficult, if not 
impossible, in states where abortion care is restricted or banned.  
For the above reasons, CalVet adamantly urges that the VA rescind RIN 2900-AS31. In 
no other circumstance must a VA patient demonstrate that their condition is life 
threatening prior to receiving coverage or care. In any other medical context, the VA 
will provide services meant to ensure that its patients remain healthy or to restore their 
health. Only in the context of reproductive health will VA patients be forced to endure 
life-altering complications due to their non-viable or high-risk pregnancies. This 
proposed rule will cause delays in access to appropriate medical care resulting in a 
myriad of tragic outcomes. Individuals who have risked their lives serving this country 
should not again be forced to endanger their lives before they are permitted to 
receive essential healthcare services. CalVet takes honoring the commitments we 
have made to caring for our nation’s veterans seriously and demands that this 
administration reconsider implementing a treacherous barrier to accessing critical 
medical services. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Lindsey Sin 
 
Secretary
